comments.author: Matthew Coombs
comments.comment: The missing axis is variance under tool use: a model can look strong on static evals and still fail when retries, schema drift, and partial tool outputs enter the loop. I usually separate selection into three tests: answer quality, recovery quality, and cost per completed task, because the last one changes the ranking fast. Which of those three has been the biggest blocker in your enterprise rollouts? #AgenticAI

comments.author: Daily Dose of Data Science
comments.comment: The scope abstraction is the part I’d watch closely. Most agent failures at company scale are not model failures, they are identity, permission, memory, and tool-state failures crossing boundaries they should not cross. Durable sandboxes also change the eval surface: now you need to test not just one run, but what the agent leaves behind for the next run.

comments.author: David García Bedoya
comments.comment: The coordination point is where most agent systems either become useful or noisy. My rule of thumb: give agents narrow ownership, require machine-checkable specs at the handoff, and keep humans on calls where the cost of a false positive is high. Curious how many teams are measuring agent work by accepted diffs/tests passed instead of tasks started?

comments.author: Raahul Seshadri
comments.comment: The gap I keep seeing is that most agent failures are not model failures, they are product and systems failures wearing an AI label. A simple agent needs boring things done well: idempotency, retries, timeouts, auth boundaries, eval gates, traceability, and a clean way to say “I don’t know.” The real question is: how many AI builders can debug the system when the demo stops being the happy path?
